content_voiceover: This slide covers delta thalassemia and delta beta thalassemia, both exam favorites more for the diagnostic pitfalls they create than for causing disease themselves. Delta thalassemia alone, mutations causing reduced, delta plus, or absent, delta zero, delta globin production, has no clinical relevance by itself, because delta chains only contribute to the small HbA2 fraction. The testable point is what happens when delta thalassemia coexists with a beta thalassemia mutation on the other allele: it pulls HbA2 down into the normal or borderline range, masking the beta thalassemia trait diagnosis, since an HbA2 of 3.5 percent or higher is exactly the number you use to diagnose beta thalassemia trait. So if you see a classic thalassemic red cell picture, low MCV, but a deceptively normal HbA2, think about co-inherited delta thalassemia. Delta beta thalassemia is a different lesion, typically a larger gene deletion, where both delta and beta globin production are reduced or absent together. The compensatory response is a variable increase in gamma chain, that is fetal hemoglobin, synthesis, but this compensation is only partial, so it does not fully balance the chain deficiency, leaving a thalassemia intermedia like phenotype with elevated HbF.
keypoints: δ-thalassemia alone: no clinical relevance — δ chains form only a tiny HbA2 fraction
δ-thal plus β-thal trait → HbA2 falsely normal/borderline → masks β-thal trait diagnosis
δβ-thalassemia: reduced/absent δ AND β chains, usually from a larger gene deletion
Compensatory ↑ γ-chain (HbF) is only partial, so a thalassemic phenotype persists
keypoint_voiceover: Remember delta thalassemia mainly as a diagnostic trap. On its own it causes nothing clinically, but paired with a beta thalassemia mutation, it drags HbA2 down into the normal range and can hide the diagnosis of beta thalassemia trait, that is the number one testable fact here. Delta beta thalassemia is a separate, larger deletion knocking out both delta and beta globin genes together, and the body responds by upregulating gamma chain, fetal hemoglobin, production, but that compensation is only partial, so patients still show a thalassemic phenotype with an HbF predominant picture.
